posts.note: 82-word podcast blurb re-releasing an April 2020 episode; no forward-looking claims.
NFT/metaverse essay. Voice may be Carlene MacMillan's ('Harvard-trained', 'just turned 40'); photo caption shows both doctors. Several own-project plans are CONTROL candidates.
Suicide-reporting guidelines essay; mostly past analysis, guidelines and advice. First-person plural; voice unclear.
Dense forecast post on consequences of Roe being overturned: EMTALA/ERISA enforcement, physician flight, employer tax liability, lawsuits.
Long defense/analysis of Cerebral; mostly present-tense argument about base rates and stimulants. Few forward-looking claims.
Co-signed O. Scott Muir + Carlene MacMillan. Heavy sarcasm about the 988 launch; one sarcastic passage logged with sincere=false.

Signed Owen Muir. Ends with an explicit 'predictions, or perhaps ... prophecies' list about an 'Elon Musk for Healthcare' (EMH); every bullet logged. 'PrimeHealth' is the author's pseudonym for a real payer.
22-word podcast blurb ('A maiden voyage'); no forward-looking claims.

statements.quote: Now, I believe they represent endless possibilities when it comes to building online communities, establishing identities and transforming industries, including the mental health industry.
statements.context: Opening section of the NFT/metaverse essay (post dated 2021-08-21). 'They' are NFTs (non-fungible tokens). The author's view shifted from 'weird art things' to a belief that NFTs will transform industries, including the mental health industry.
statements.note: Borderline: a belief about potential, not a dated call. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: I think more and more NFT projects will include charitable giving as part of their roadmap.
statements.context: After describing Blazed Cats (about $250,000 raised for Mental Health America in under 3 weeks) and Alpha Betty Doodles (donations to teachers via DonorsChoose). Trend call that charitable giving becomes a common part of NFT project roadmaps.
statements.note: Trend call with no date.

statements.quote: Blazed Cats caught my attention because in under 3 weeks since launching, they raised around a quarter of a million dollars for Mental Health America and are just getting started.
statements.context: Section 'Blazed Cats- Show those Penguins the Way!'. The Blazed Cats NFT project raised about $250,000 for Mental Health America in under 3 weeks; 'just getting started' implies continued fundraising and growth.
statements.note: Borderline: implied continuation claim ('just getting started'); the rest is a past fact.

statements.quote: we recognize for individuals like sex workers who are often excluded from traditional banking systems (and, come October, OnlyFans too), crypto offers a better alternative
statements.context: Aside in a paragraph about Brooklyn Minds (the authors' practice) accepting cryptocurrency for years. The aside states that from October (2021) OnlyFans will also exclude sex workers, restating OnlyFans's announced policy change as a coming fact.
statements.note: Dated call embedded in an aside; restates an announced third-party policy change as fact.

statements.quote: We have plans for a generative NFT project of our own focusing on generic medications with a much lower single price point but know to get these projects right and not have a Stoner Cats-esque mishap, we need the right team.
statements.context: Section 'Psychiatrists of the Metaverse'. The Frontier Psychiatrists minted a first NFT ('Esketamine in Space', Drug Holiday collection, on OpenSea) and plan a generative NFT project about generic medications at a lower price point, once they have the right team.
statements.note: Own-project plan; coder may mark CONTROL. Conditional on assembling a team.

statements.quote: We plan to have a portion of the proceeds donated to mental health charities and to a scholarship fund for individuals in our own practice who cannot afford to pay for the innovative service we offer.
statements.context: Plan for the proceeds of the authors' own generative NFT project (Drug Holiday series): donations to mental health charities and a scholarship fund for patients of their practice (Brooklyn Minds).
statements.note: Own-project plan; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: a child psychiatrist who has held leadership positions there and at the American Psychiatric Association messaged me the other day jokingly asking if I wanted to start a psychiatric practice in the metaverse with him. The thing is, I am not joking!
statements.context: 'There' is the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (AACAP), which had liked the author's Blazed Cats tweet. The author signals real intent to start a psychiatric practice in the metaverse; the next section is titled 'Psychiatrists of the Metaverse'.
entities: American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
statements.note: Borderline: stated intent, not a forecast. Own activity; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Paid subscribers of our Substack will have access to the full audio of our show soon as well.
statements.context: Closing section. The full audio of the Clubhouse show 'NFTs for Mental Health' will be released to paid subscribers of The Frontier Psychiatrists Substack.
statements.note: Own-newsletter commitment; low forecast value; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: I certainly hope that is changing and that coverage will continue to improve when suicides do occur.
statements.context: Section 'What can you do to help?'. Journalists told the author they got little training on reporting suicide in journalism school or from editors. The author hopes training is changing and that media coverage of suicides will keep improving against the 16 best-practice guidelines.
statements.note: Wish framing ('hope') with a predictive clause; logged as borderline for recall.

statements.quote: While our New Frontiers season is over, we have ongoing conversations on Clubhouse, including an AMA with the Frontier Psychiatrists and other mental health experts every Sunday night at 7pm EDT.
statements.context: Closing note. The New Frontiers Clubhouse show season has ended; the Sphere Mental Health Club continues with a weekly Sunday 7pm EDT AMA with the Frontier Psychiatrists.
statements.note: Own-schedule commitment; low forecast value; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: This is only the first shot. ERISA is next.
statements.context: July 2 (2022) update atop the post. The author says the Department of Justice sued Ohio that day over EMTALA violations and predicts ERISA-based federal action follows; the Department of Labor had 'weighed in' in Massachusetts on fiduciary violations under ERISA the week before.
statements.note: Predicts an enforcement sequence: EMTALA suit first, ERISA action next.

statements.quote: Enforcement is coming. This is not a drill.
statements.context: Same July 2 update. Federal enforcement (EMTALA, then ERISA fiduciary rules) against states and employers after the decision overturning Roe v. Wade is asserted as imminent.
statements.note: No date given.

statements.quote: Turning back the clock fifty years on Roe will lead to similarly catastrophic outcomes—physician shortages, dead patients beyond those seeking abortions, and tax liability for large employers in impacted states.
statements.context: Thesis of the July 1 essay, via an H. G. Wells 'Time Machine' analogy. Predicted consequences of Roe v. Wade being overturned: physician shortages, deaths beyond abortion seekers, and tax liability for large employers in states with abortion bans.
statements.note: Compound claim with three testable parts.

statements.quote: Violating standards invites malpractice lawsuits. Therefore, were the law for post-operative chest-stabbing passed, it would create a problem for the medical malpractice carriers covering surgeons. Families would sue, and win.
statements.context: Hypothetical analogy: a law mandating surgeons stab patients stands in for abortion bans that force doctors to violate standards of care. Underlying claim: bans will create problems for malpractice carriers, and families will sue doctors and win.
statements.note: Fictional analogy; the underlying claim about bans and malpractice carriers reads as sincere.

statements.quote: Once you mandate malpractice, you create uninsurable doctors. Uninsured doctors won’t practice in states withs bans.
statements.context: Mechanism claim: abortion bans mandate malpractice, which makes doctors uninsurable; uninsurable doctors will not practice in ban states. ('withs' is the author's typo.)
statements.note: Chain of causal forecasts; see the following statements from the same paragraph.

statements.quote: So, as soon as patients sue doctors who can’t follow established medical guidelines, doctors will flee those states.
statements.context: Predicted physician flight from abortion-ban states once malpractice suits over withheld standard care begin. Author notes most doctors carry debt and need insurable practice.
statements.note: Conditional on lawsuits starting.

statements.quote: When you create gaps in doctor availability, you end up with health plans that don’t provide comprehensive medical care. No one can legally sell these, or buy them.
statements.context: Next link in the chain: doctor shortages make health plans in ban states non-comprehensive, and such plans cannot legally be sold or bought (ERISA fiduciary argument). Author notes employers already buy plane tickets as a workaround.
statements.note: Mechanism forecast; legal-interpretation claim in the second sentence.

statements.quote: This problem becomes worse over time— not enough OB/GYN‘s means no med school education in such states.
statements.context: The doctor-availability gap in abortion-ban states is predicted to compound: too few OB/GYNs means medical education in those states collapses.
statements.note: Long-horizon compounding claim.

statements.quote: Now, every employer who has any employees in any state that bans abortion owes the IRS on every penny they spend on health benefits for their employees. This is a problem for virtually all large employers.
statements.context: Legal argument: under ERISA and the 2021 appropriations act fiduciary mandate (author: 'Combined Appropriations Act of 2021'), plans that do not cover medically necessary care, including abortion, lose the tax exemption, so employers with staff in ban states owe tax on health benefits.
statements.note: Present-tense legal interpretation; the testable part is whether employers in ban states actually face IRS liability or lose the exemption.

statements.quote: In the wreckage that follows, doctors can’t practice for lack of insurance, patients can’t get medical care they need, and employers have a massive tax bill if they try to provide insurance.
statements.context: Jenga analogy: Roe v. Wade as the bottom block of legal precedent. Compound forecast of consequences after its removal: uninsurable doctors, patients without care, employers with a massive tax bill.
statements.note: Compound claim; restates earlier calls in the same post.

statements.quote: There are a hell of a lot of lawsuits coming. This will be catastrophic for most patients, their employers, doctors– and even insurance conglomerates.
statements.context: Closing paragraph. A wave of lawsuits is predicted after Roe's overturn, catastrophic for patients, employers, doctors and insurers.
statements.note: Two parts: many lawsuits coming; catastrophic effect on four groups.

statements.quote: Buckle up. It’s going to get bumpy.
statements.context: Final lines of the post; generic warning of turbulence after Roe's overturn.
statements.note: Vague; logged for recall.

statements.quote: The only thing I will say about this particular interview, is that she asked one really important question about controlled substance prescribing. It led to her stepping away from the interview process before any non-disclosure agreement was signed: “What are you going to do if the Ryan-Haight Act gets reinstated?”
statements.context: Part 1. A colleague interviewing for Cerebral's Chief Medical Officer role (before Softbank funded Cerebral) asked what Cerebral would do if the Ryan-Haight Act (in-person requirement for controlled-substance prescribing, suspended during COVID) is reinstated. Executives answered 'We hope it doesn't!', which the author calls unsatisfactory.
statements.note: Colleague's question; author endorses the risk as real ('not a satisfactory answer'). Borderline: a question, not a stated forecast.

statements.quote: This is a huge problem. But it’s not a problem Cerebral can solve even with the most aggressive messages from bubbly recruiters on LinkedIn.
statements.context: Part 6. Workforce shortage: about 30,000 US psychiatrists vs about 5.7M diagnosed bipolar patients; most mental illness is treated by primary care or mid-level clinicians. The author says Cerebral cannot solve the specialist shortage despite $462M raised.
statements.confidence_phrase: not a problem Cerebral can solve
statements.note: Capability denial; borderline forward-looking.

statements.quote: And every single one of the incidents reported was done by someone who was unable to be tracked previously, and after they leave Cerebral are highly unlikely to have their practice tracked thereafter.
statements.context: Part 6, on Cerebral's 2,060 incident reports in seven months of 2021. The clinicians involved were untracked before Cerebral and, the author predicts, will be untracked again after leaving.
statements.note: Claim about the practice environment clinicians return to; hard to resolve.

statements.quote: They’re probably charging more now after leaving Cerebral and many will not continue to take insurance in solo practice.
statements.context: Part 6. Clinicians who left Cerebral: the author expects they still treat patients, charge more, and that many will stop taking insurance in solo practice.
statements.note: Present hedge ('probably') plus a future call on insurance participation.

statements.quote: Cerebral may be guilty of a variety of regulatory and other missteps or crimes—we will find out soon enough.
statements.context: Part 7, near the end. The author hedges on whether Cerebral committed regulatory violations or crimes and expects the answer soon, with investigations and reporting under way.
statements.note: Hedged both ways; the testable part is that a determination on Cerebral's conduct arrives 'soon enough'.

statements.quote: how does this actually move the needle on mental health services in the United States? Spoiler alert: It doesn’t- at least not right now.
statements.context: Opening on the July 16, 2022 launch of the 988 crisis number. The authors say it does not move the needle on US mental health services, at least for now, since it only shortens the number for the existing National Suicide Prevention Lifeline.
statements.note: Present/near-term assessment; borderline forward-looking. Co-authored post (Muir + MacMillan).

statements.quote: We now feel so much more hopeful that they won’t close the local money losing psych inpatient unit, that insurance will start fairly compensating mental health professionals and that the police who show up to help a mentally ill black or brown patient won’t shoot them. Easy as 1-2-3! Or rather 9-8-8!
statements.context: Sarcastic passage about the 988 launch. The literal 'hopeful' claims are the inverse of the authors' expectation: 988 will not stop inpatient unit closures, will not fix insurer reimbursement of mental health professionals, and will not reduce police shootings of mentally ill Black and brown patients.
statements.note: Sarcasm; sincere=false for the literal claim. The sincere reading is the negation of each clause.

statements.quote: We call bullshit that any of our patients will be meaningfully impacted in the near term by this change.
statements.context: Section 'Help is Not on the Way'. The authors predict the 988 rollout will not meaningfully affect any of their patients in the near term.
statements.confidence_phrase: We call bullshit that ... will be
statements.note: Own-patient framing, but a general near-term impact call on 988.

statements.quote: While this initial funding push will help, serious doubts exist if it will be sustained or enough to meet increased demand caused by publicizing the new 988 number.
statements.context: 988 budget: $282M in 2021 and $150M in 2022 for an understaffed Lifeline (1 in 6 calls disconnected before reaching a counselor). The authors expect the funding to help but doubt it will be sustained or sufficient for demand created by publicity.
statements.note: Compound: funding helps (positive) plus doubt on sustainability and adequacy (negative).

statements.quote: Starting on July 16, however, the caller may logically think to themselves “Oh I should call that new mental health number about this suicidal crisis!” and dial 988. That would be wrong. Calling the wrong number wastes precious time your loved one’s poisoned liver does not have as the crisis counselor needs to redirect you to 911 and get an ambulance dispatched.
statements.context: Predicted harm from splitting 'medical' (911) and 'mental health' (988) emergencies: callers facing a Tylenol overdose may dial 988 instead of 911 and lose time; 988 also lacks 911's geolocation and routes by area code.
statements.note: Hedged mechanism forecast about misrouting of overdose calls.

statements.quote: Until we reform the public policies that have abandoned them there, these tragic outcomes will continue.
statements.context: Quote from 'Snook' of the Treatment Advocacy Center, cited by the authors as evidence that people with untreated mental illness (17x greater likelihood of being killed by police) will keep dying in law enforcement encounters until policy reform.
statements.horizon_text: Until we reform the public policies
statements.note: Third-party quote (Snook, Treatment Advocacy Center) presented approvingly; own_claim set true as an endorsed restatement.

statements.quote: 988 can save lives too if more effort and funding is directed at what happens when the callers needing more help than the line on its own hang up the phone.
statements.context: Conditional near the end: 988 can save lives if downstream services (what happens after the call) get funding and effort; otherwise it is like a 'Fire Support Hotline' while the house burns.
statements.note: Conditional positive call.

statements.quote: We are waiting for our Elon Musk for Healthcare (EMH for short). I’ll set the stage, make my case for Elon the Visionary, and describe what EMH will look like when she arrives.
statements.context: Opening, after Amazon's $3.9B acquisition of One Medical. Umbrella premise of the post: a visionary healthcare leader ('Elon Musk for Healthcare', EMH) will arrive; the closing 'prophecies' list describes her.
statements.note: Presupposes the arrival of an EMH; specific traits are logged from the closing list.

statements.quote: Honestly, LifeStance investors, really? I don’t have any money and I’m still buying put options on this roll up with zero market strategy. You are aware that every clinician can make more money elsewhere the next day, right?
statements.context: Market-cap comparison of 'BS companies' vs 'Real Companies'. LifeStance (a behavioral-health roll-up) is the first 'BS company'; the author says he is buying put options on it because clinicians can leave for better pay at any time.
statements.note: Implied bearish call via a stated put-option position; no explicit price or date.

statements.quote: Every other adorable, scrappy start up company, issuing lovable press releases every day… is but a poor player strutting and fretting their hour up on the stage until either failure or acquisition. And both of those outcomes are determined by the Real Companies at the BUCA level...or Amazon level.
statements.context: Section 'The Deciders': mega-payers (BUCA, the big four insurers) and Amazon price, pay and decide; every healthcare startup ends in failure or acquisition at their discretion. Even Cerebral at a $4.5B valuation is called 'cute' next to them.
statements.note: Structural prediction: all healthcare startups end in failure or acquisition decided by mega-payers or Amazon.

statements.quote: Pro Tip: never, ever, ever name your company Done . It’s just asking for trouble in a Greek Tragedy kinda way.
statements.context: Aside after an embedded clip about a 'displeasing entity' being 'terminated from all systems'. Done (an ADHD telehealth prescriber) is implied to be headed for a hubris-driven downfall.
statements.note: Joke framing; the underlying expectation (Done faces a bad end) reads as semi-sincere. Borderline.

statements.quote: The game IS rigged for medical innovators. That isn’t changing for us…unless we gradually take over the leadership of these endeavors ? Nah. I’m kidding. They will never risk their profits!
statements.context: After recounting his own company's lost 'PrimeHealth' contract (PrimeHealth is the author's pseudonym for a real large payer). The author predicts the market stays rigged against medical innovators and incumbents will never risk their profits.
statements.note: Negative structural call; 'PrimeHealth' is a fictionalized name.

statements.quote: Without real, serious companies—with bold Jeff-named founders—ready to deploy massive resources to change market fundamentals, this can’t happen.
statements.context: Conditional: changing healthcare market fundamentals requires mega-companies at Amazon/Jeff Bezos scale deploying massive resources; without them, the position of medical innovators does not change.
statements.note: Conditional necessity claim.

statements.quote: That’s it. That’s the sum total of why I think Elon Musk and his approach with Tesla, SpaceX, the Boring Company, and who knows what next, will win transportation.
statements.context: Section on Elon Musk as the archetype visionary: his market insight (point A to point B faster and easier) plus tunnels, cars, batteries and satellites means Musk's companies will 'win transportation'.
statements.note: Outside healthcare; explicit call on Musk's companies.

statements.quote: Visionaries will disrupt the living daylights out of that kind of thinking.
statements.context: Section 'Taking Physics Seriously': regulators and 'Nervous Nellies' block flying, self-driving and tunnels; the author predicts visionaries will disrupt that regulatory mindset.
statements.note: Vague; logged for recall.

statements.quote: EMH will have this restraint. She will see the future, but not tell us more than we are ready to hear.
statements.context: After the Overton Window argument (sell the believable next step, not the far future). Predicted trait of the coming Elon Musk for Healthcare (EMH).
statements.note: Trait prediction about a hypothetical future leader; hard to resolve.

statements.quote: Our visionary leader will have a market insight. It will be breathtakingly simple.
statements.context: Item 1 of the closing 'predictions, or perhaps ... prophecies' list about the Elon Musk for Healthcare (EMH).
statements.note: Prophecies list; mock-biblical framing but presented as the author's predictions.

statements.quote: Elon Musk for Healthcare (EMH) will not be a 22 year old 1st time start-up founder.
statements.context: Item 2 of the prophecies list: healthcare is too complicated for a first-time 22-year-old founder to find the simple insight; experience is needed.
statements.note: Negative trait call.

statements.quote: EMH will probably not be actual Elon Musk. He would have talked about health care more. He talks about everything else.
statements.context: Item 3 of the prophecies list.
statements.note: Hedged negative call on a named person.

statements.quote: I also don’t think Jeff Bezos is the chosen one. Time will tell, but he’s more likely in the running for Darth Vader/Anakin Skywalker of healthcare. Jeff is our Savior’s dad at best, and his redemption is similarly nigh.
statements.context: Item 4 of the prophecies list, days after Amazon's One Medical deal: Bezos is not the visionary healthcare leader; more likely a villain-then-redeemed figure.
statements.confidence_phrase: I also don’t think ... more likely
statements.note: Star Wars framing; sincere core: Bezos/Amazon will not be the transformative healthcare leader.

statements.quote: She— who is coming to Disrupt Healthcare as Elon disrupted our batteries— is likely to be from outside PrimeHealth. It’s hard to see the Matrix from within.
statements.context: Item 5 of the prophecies list: EMH will likely come from outside 'PrimeHealth' (pseudonym for a large incumbent payer).
statements.note: Hedged origin call.

statements.quote: She, of whom we were forewarned by a Frontier Psychiatrist , will have a Compelling Story of Lived Experience of a Serious Health Condition. Of this, we will learn on a special episode of the JRE .
statements.context: Item 6 of the prophecies list: EMH will have a lived-experience story of serious illness, revealed on the Joe Rogan Experience (JRE); Rogan's lack of libertarian dismissal will mark her as the true EMH.
statements.note: Lived-experience part reads sincere; the JRE/Rogan detail is satirical.

statements.quote: She will have died (in the fire-y wreck of a startup?) in yet another move “towards value based care” that was smote by the Wrath of the one true Payer ?). Praise be Layoffs.fyi , she is Born Again in a new leadership role, and harken unto the good word as told in a Forbes puff-piece shared all across the LinkedIn lands, the fit will be better.
statements.context: Item 7 of the prophecies list, EMH's backstory: a failed value-based-care startup killed by a dominant payer, then a new leadership role announced via a Forbes piece shared on LinkedIn.
statements.note: Mock-prophetic framing; core claim (EMH emerges from a failed value-based-care startup) reads as the author's expectation.

statements.quote: Her funding, blessed be, will likely be from sources both smart and unorthodox . I mean, Annie Lamont will also get in early, cause Oak HC/FT just raised a 5th fund. Is saying no to Oak HC/FT even allowed anymore?
statements.context: Item 8 of the prophecies list: EMH's funding will likely be smart and unorthodox, and Annie Lamont / Oak HC/FT (which just raised a fifth fund) will invest early.
statements.note: Two parts: unorthodox funding sources; Oak HC/FT gets in early.

statements.quote: She will be rumored to have had experiences with psychedelic medicine (honestly this is just playing the numbers at this point), and some will believe from this experience, insights came to make the world a better place.
statements.context: Item 9 of the prophecies list: EMH will be rumored to have used psychedelic medicine; the author notes this is 'playing the numbers' given how common it is.
statements.note: Half-joking base-rate call.

statements.quote: She will destroy all those who came before by the end of her rule, including PrimeHealth.
statements.context: Item 10, the final prophecy: EMH will destroy incumbent healthcare companies including 'PrimeHealth' (pseudonym for a real large payer). The post closes: 'Thus, it was foretold, and thus it will be.'
statements.horizon_text: by the end of her rule
statements.note: Grandiose mock-prophecy; treated as the author's stated expectation.
